sections.title: A fly in the urinal
sections.intro_md:
Somewhere in Amsterdam's Schiphol airport in the early 1990s, a cleaning manager had an idea that sounds like a joke. Etch a small black housefly into each men's urinal, just left of the drain. Men aim at things. Aim at the fly and less ends up on the floor.

It worked well enough that the fly spread to airports, stadiums and offices around the world.

That field, **behavioural economics**, won Nobel prizes in 2002 and 2017, moved trillions in pension savings, put more than 200 'nudge units' inside governments in dozens of countries, and gave regulators, from Washington to India's SEBI, a new vocabulary for what goes wrong when people choose. It also hit a credibility crisis.

spotlights.name: The Schiphol urinal fly
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny black fly printed on the porcelain near the drain of a men's urinal.
spotlights.story_md: The fly is usually credited to Aad Kieboom, who managed Schiphol's cleaning, though he said the idea came from a colleague, Jos van Bedaf, who remembered soldiers aiming at targets painted in army urinals in the 1960s. The fly cost almost nothing and asked nothing of anyone: no signs, no fines, no lecture. Kieboom later told NPR that spillage fell by 80 percent. That number became famous. It is also shaky: Kieboom said it was 'very empirical', no published study has been found, and a urinal researcher put the likely effect nearer 50 percent. The fly is real. The statistic is folklore.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the cleanest picture of a 'nudge': change the setting, not the rules, and behaviour shifts.
spotlights.memory_hook: Men aim. Give them a fly.

spotlights.name: Thaler's Nobel, and his joke about the money
spotlights.spot_it: Richard Thaler, white-haired and grinning, at the 2017 Nobel ceremonies in Stockholm.
spotlights.story_md: When the Royal Swedish Academy announced the 2017 economics prize, about 9 million Swedish kronor, for Richard Thaler's 'contributions to behavioural economics', reporters asked what he would do with the money. 'I will try to spend it as irrationally as possible,' he said. The joke was a lesson. In standard theory money has no labels: a kronor from a prize is the same as a kronor from a salary. Thaler's research on **mental accounting** showed that people do label money, into windfalls, rent, treats and savings, and spend each pot differently. Later he gave the straight answer: some fun, the rest to good causes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Nobel made a once-fringe field official.
spotlights.memory_hook: Money has no labels. People stick labels on anyway.

sections.title: What it is, in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Classical economics works with a useful fiction: **Homo economicus**, a person who knows what they want, weighs every option, never tires, never envies and never procrastinates. Behavioural economics keeps the maths but swaps in a real human, borrowing evidence from psychology.

The core findings fit in a sentence each. Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please. Defaults stick, because doing nothing is the easiest choice. The way an option is framed changes which one people pick. People care about fairness and will pay to punish unfairness. Today's self beats tomorrow's self in most arguments about saving, eating and exercise.

The policy offshoot is **nudging**: designing the 'choice architecture' so the easy option is the good one, while leaving every option open.

spotlights.name: Homo economicus, the rational agent
spotlights.when: Named in the late 1800s; idea from John Stuart Mill, 1836
spotlights.spot_it: Any model in which people have stable preferences, perfect willpower and unlimited attention.
spotlights.story_md: John Stuart Mill described political economy as studying man as 'a being who desires to possess wealth', setting other motives aside on purpose. Critics later mocked this figure as 'economic man', and the Latin label stuck. The simplification was powerful: assume people maximise and you can predict how markets clear, how taxes bite and how prices move. Behavioural economists never claimed the model was useless. Their point was narrower and more damaging: people deviate from it in ways that are **systematic**, not random, so the errors do not cancel out. If everyone overweights small risks in the same direction, insurance markets and pension systems will look different from the textbook.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every finding today is measured against this imaginary person.
spotlights.memory_hook: Economics had a robot. Psychology brought a human.

spotlights.name: Fast and slow thinking
spotlights.when: Popularised in Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011
spotlights.spot_it: Two modes of thought: quick, automatic intuition and slow, effortful reasoning.
spotlights.story_md: Kahneman's 2011 bestseller organised decades of findings around two characters. 'System 1' is fast, automatic and always on: it reads faces, finishes the phrase 'bread and', and jumps to conclusions. 'System 2' is slow and lazy: it does long multiplication and checks System 1's work, when it bothers. Try the bat-and-ball puzzle: a bat and a ball cost 1.10 dollars together, and the bat costs 1 dollar more than the ball. Most people's first answer for the ball is 10 cents. The right answer is 5 cents.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave the public one simple frame for all the biases.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten cents is System 1. Five cents is System 2.

sections.title: Before it had a name
sections.intro_md:
The idea that people are not perfectly rational is older than economics as a profession. Adam Smith wrote about it in 1759. Keynes built 'animal spirits' into his 1936 theory of slumps. What changed after the Second World War was that economics became mathematical, and the maths needed tidy agents.

A few people pushed back with **experiments**, not just complaints. In 1953 Maurice Allais showed that respected colleagues violated expected utility on simple bets. In 1955 Herbert Simon argued that real minds have limited time and attention, so they 'satisfice' instead of optimising. In 1961 a young RAND analyst, Daniel Ellsberg, found that people dislike not knowing the odds even more than they dislike risk. Each was treated as a curiosity. Together they were the cracks the later field widened.

spotlights.name: Adam Smith's other book
spotlights.spot_it: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, written 17 years before The Wealth of Nations.
spotlights.story_md: Most people know Smith for the 'invisible hand' of self-interest. His first book is about something else: sympathy, conscience and the 'impartial spectator' inside each of us. Read today it sounds like a behavioural economics textbook. Smith wrote that 'we suffer more' when we fall from a better situation to a worse one 'than we ever enjoy when we rise from a worse to a better'. That is loss aversion, about 220 years before Kahneman and Tversky measured it. A 2005 paper by Ashraf, Camerer and Loewenstein was titled, simply, 'Adam Smith, Behavioral Economist'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The founder of economics never believed in Homo economicus.
spotlights.memory_hook: The invisible hand had a conscience in the other book.

spotlights.name: Keynes and 'animal spirits'
spotlights.spot_it: The phrase economists use when confidence, not calculation, drives investment.
spotlights.story_md: In The General Theory, John Maynard Keynes argued that most decisions to invest can only be taken 'as the result of animal spirits', a spontaneous urge to action rather than a weighted average of benefits and probabilities. Nobody really knows what a railway or a mine will earn in ten years, he said, so investment rides on mood. When confidence collapses, spending collapses, and an economy can sit in a slump for years. George Akerlof and Robert Shiller revived the phrase for a 2009 book after the financial crisis. Behavioural macroeconomics starts here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It linked psychology to booms and slumps, not just to shopping.
spotlights.memory_hook: Investment runs on mood as much as maths.

spotlights.name: The Allais paradox
spotlights.spot_it: Two pairs of bets on which most people choose in a way expected-utility theory says is inconsistent.
spotlights.story_md: At a 1952 conference in Paris, the French economist Maurice Allais handed leading decision theorists a pair of choices. In the first, most preferred a sure million francs over a gamble with a tiny chance of nothing. In the second, with the certainty removed, most switched to the riskier option. Both choices cannot fit expected utility theory, because the two pairs differ only by a common slice of probability. The lesson, later called the **certainty effect**, is that a sure thing carries a special premium in the mind.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that certainty is weighted differently from high probability.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sure money is worth more than its odds.

spotlights.name: Herbert Simon and 'satisficing'
spotlights.spot_it: A polymath at Carnegie Mellon who won both the economics Nobel and computing's Turing Award.
spotlights.story_md: Herbert Simon thought the rational agent asked too much of a human brain. In 'A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice' (1955, first drafted at RAND) he argued that people have limited information, limited time and limited computing power, so they look for an option that is good enough and stop. He called it **satisficing**, a blend of satisfy and suffice, and the wider idea **bounded rationality**. Simon won the 1978 economics Nobel for research on decision-making inside organisations, and was a founder of artificial intelligence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first Nobel for a behavioural idea, a generation early.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not the best house: the first good-enough house.

spotlights.name: The Ellsberg paradox
spotlights.spot_it: Two urns, one with a known mix of balls and one unknown: people bet on the known one.
spotlights.story_md: In 1961 Daniel Ellsberg, a RAND analyst with a Harvard PhD in progress, published 'Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms'. Offer people a bet on drawing a red ball from an urn with 50 red and 50 black, or from an urn with 100 balls in an unknown mix. Most prefer the known urn, whichever colour they bet on, which no single set of beliefs can justify. The finding, **ambiguity aversion**, explains why investors flee the unfamiliar. Ellsberg's later fame came from elsewhere: in 1971 he leaked the secret Pentagon history of the Vietnam war, the Pentagon Papers, to the New York Times. He died in June 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It split 'risk' (known odds) from 'ambiguity' (unknown odds).
spotlights.memory_hook: The decision theorist who leaked the Pentagon Papers.

sections.title: Two Israelis and a pencil
sections.intro_md:
The modern field begins with a friendship. In 1969 Daniel Kahneman, a psychologist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, invited a colleague, Amos Tversky, to talk to his graduate seminar. They argued, then started working together, often writing at a single desk and talking for hours a day.

Their method was disarmingly simple: pose short questions to students and experts, record the answers, and find the **systematic** mistakes. In 1974 a paper in Science named three mental shortcuts, representativeness, availability and anchoring. In 1979 they published **prospect theory** in Econometrica, a theory of how people actually choose between risky options. It became the most cited paper the journal has ever printed.

Tversky died of cancer in 1996, aged 59. Nobel prizes are not given posthumously, so in 2002 Kahneman, a psychologist who never took an economics course, shared the economics prize alone for their joint work.

spotlights.name: Daniel Kahneman
spotlights.spot_it: A slight, soft-spoken psychologist with heavy glasses, usually photographed mid-sentence.
spotlights.story_md: Kahneman spent his childhood in occupied Paris as a Jewish boy hiding from the Nazis, moved to Palestine in 1948, and built the Israeli army's personnel interview system as a young officer; a version of it was used for decades. As a psychologist he was famous for doubting his own ideas. With Tversky he mapped the errors of intuition; later he studied happiness, separating the 'experiencing self' from the 'remembering self'. His 2002 Nobel citation praised him for 'having integrated insights from psychological research into economic science'. He died on 27 March 2024, aged 90.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned 'people make mistakes' into a measurable science.
spotlights.memory_hook: A psychologist who won economics' top prize.

spotlights.name: Amos Tversky
spotlights.spot_it: Kahneman's partner: a paratrooper, mathematician and the quickest mind in most rooms.
spotlights.story_md: Tversky was a decorated Israeli paratrooper and a mathematical psychologist who moved to Stanford in 1978. Colleagues joked about the 'Tversky intelligence test': the faster you realised he was smarter than you, the smarter you were. He brought formal rigour to Kahneman's intuitions, and the pair wrote so closely that they flipped a coin for the order of names. Their partnership cooled in the 1980s when Tversky received most of the public credit, a story Michael Lewis told in The Undoing Project (2016). Tversky died in 1996 at 59. Kahneman always said the prize was, in effect, a joint one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Half of the most influential partnership in social science.
spotlights.memory_hook: They flipped a coin to decide whose name came first.

spotlights.name: Prospect theory
spotlights.spot_it: An S-shaped value curve, steeper for losses than for gains, centred on a reference point.
spotlights.story_md: Prospect theory replaced expected utility with three ideas. First, people judge outcomes as **gains or losses from a reference point**, usually the status quo, not as final wealth. Second, losses loom larger than gains: the curve is steeper below zero. Third, people treat probabilities unevenly, overweighting small chances (lottery tickets, insurance against rare disasters) and underweighting near-certainties. Together these explain why the same person buys insurance and lottery tickets, and why framing a choice as losses makes people gamble. A 2024 meta-analysis of 607 estimates put the average loss aversion coefficient at about 1.96: a loss counts roughly twice as much as an equal gain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the single most important model in the field.
spotlights.memory_hook: Losing 100 hurts like winning 200 feels.

spotlights.name: The rigged wheel of fortune
spotlights.spot_it: A numbered wheel spun before a quiz question, and answers that drift toward the number.
spotlights.story_md: Tversky and Kahneman built a wheel of fortune marked 0 to 100 but rigged to stop only at 10 or 65. Students at the University of Oregon watched it spin, wrote down the number, and were asked whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than it, then to estimate the real figure. Those who saw 10 gave a median estimate of 25 percent. Those who saw 65 said 45 percent. A number they knew was random dragged their judgment. This is **anchoring**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Any first number in a negotiation is doing work.
spotlights.memory_hook: Spin 10, guess 25. Spin 65, guess 45.

sections.title: The mind's shortcuts, and where they fail
sections.intro_md:
A **heuristic** is a mental shortcut: a quick rule that usually gives a decent answer. A **bias** is the predictable direction in which that shortcut goes wrong. The heuristics-and-biases programme catalogued dozens of them.

A few have proved robust and consequential. **Representativeness** makes us judge by resemblance, so a vivid description beats basic probability. **Framing** means that logically identical options described as lives saved or lives lost get different answers. The **planning fallacy** makes us plan for the best case, which is why big projects run late and over budget. The **sunk cost** effect keeps us pouring money into failures because we have already spent so much.

visual.title: Same choice, different words: the 'Asian disease' problem (Tversky and Kahneman 1981)

spotlights.name: Linda the bank teller
spotlights.spot_it: A short biography of 'Linda', then a question that tricks most readers into breaking a law of probability.
spotlights.story_md: Linda is 31, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy and as a student was deeply concerned with discrimination and social justice, and joined anti-nuclear demonstrations. Which is more probable: (a) Linda is a bank teller, or (b) Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement? In Tversky and Kahneman's 1983 study, about 85 percent of 142 students chose (b). But (b) can never be more likely than (a), because every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller. The description resembles a feminist, so resemblance beats arithmetic. This is the **conjunction fallacy**. Statistical training barely helped.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Detailed, plausible stories feel more likely even as they become less likely.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller.

spotlights.name: The 'Asian disease' problem
spotlights.spot_it: Two descriptions of the same public-health choice that flip most people's answer.
spotlights.story_md: A disease is expected to kill 600 people. One group of students chose between Program A, which saves 200 people for sure, and Program B, a one-in-three chance of saving all 600 and two-in-three of saving no one: 72 percent took the sure thing. A second group got the same programs described as deaths: under C, 400 people die for sure; under D, a one-in-three chance nobody dies. Now 78 percent took the gamble. A and C are identical, as are B and D. The **framing** effect: describe outcomes as gains and people play safe; describe them as losses and they gamble.
spotlights.why_it_matters: How a choice is worded can reverse it.
spotlights.memory_hook: 200 saved feels safe. 400 dead feels like a gamble worth taking.

spotlights.name: The planning fallacy and the Sydney Opera House
spotlights.spot_it: White sail-shaped roofs on Sydney harbour, and a budget that grew about fourteen-fold.
spotlights.story_md: Kahneman and Tversky named the planning fallacy in 1979: people forecast from the best-case scenario of their own plan and ignore how long similar projects took. The Sydney Opera House is the textbook case. The original estimate was about A$7 million with a four-year build. It opened in 1973, ten years late, scaled down, at about A$102 million. Guinness lists it as the largest proportional cost increase for a building project. Kahneman's fix was the **outside view**: before estimating your own project, look up how long and how much the typical comparable project took.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Infrastructure overruns are a bias problem, not just bad luck.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven million planned, 102 million paid.

spotlights.name: Concorde and the sunk cost fallacy
spotlights.spot_it: The needle-nosed supersonic airliner, flown by British Airways and Air France until 2003.
spotlights.story_md: Britain and France kept funding Concorde long after it was clear the plane would never pay back its development costs, in part because so much had already been spent and stopping felt like admitting waste. In 1976 the biologists Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle used the term 'Concorde fallacy' in Nature for animals that seem to keep investing in a lost cause, and the name stuck in economics too. Rationally, money already spent and unrecoverable should not affect the next decision. In practice people finish bad meals they paid for and sit through bad films.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ask what the next rupee buys, not what the last crore bought.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sunk money is gone. Do not follow it.

sections.title: Thaler's list of anomalies
sections.intro_md:
Kahneman and Tversky were psychologists. The person who carried their findings into economics was a not especially promising young economist at the University of Rochester. Richard Thaler kept a list on his office blackboard of things people did that the standard model said they should not, such as demanding more to sell an object than they would pay to buy it.

In 1977 he spent a year near Kahneman and Tversky at Stanford, and in 1980 he published 'Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice'. From 1987 he wrote a column, 'Anomalies', in the Journal of Economic Perspectives: 19 instalments over almost two decades, each laying out a stubborn fact the theory could not explain. The Nobel committee in 2017 named his four big contributions: mental accounting, the endowment effect, social preferences and self-control.

visual.title: What a free coffee mug is worth (median, US dollars; Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler 1990, experiment 6, Simon Fraser students)

spotlights.name: Richard Thaler
spotlights.spot_it: A cheerful economist at Chicago Booth who describes himself as lazy and calls his field 'misbehaving'.
spotlights.story_md: Thaler was born in New Jersey in 1945 and has taught at the University of Chicago since 1995, the home of free-market economics and of his fiercest critics. His memoir, Misbehaving (2015), tells the field's history as a running fight with 'Econs', the imaginary people of the textbook, as opposed to 'Humans'. He co-wrote Nudge (2008) with the law professor Cass Sunstein, consulted for the UK's Behavioural Insights Team, and made a cameo in the film The Big Short explaining the 'hot hand' fallacy with Selena Gomez at a blackjack table. His Nobel lecture began with a bowl of cashews.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made the anomalies impossible for economists to ignore.
spotlights.memory_hook: Econs versus Humans.

spotlights.name: The bowl of cashews
spotlights.spot_it: A bowl of nuts taken away before dinner, and guests who said thank you.
spotlights.story_md: As a graduate student Thaler had friends over and put out a large bowl of cashews with drinks while the roast cooked. The guests began devouring them. Worried about their appetites, he took the bowl into the kitchen. Everyone was relieved. Then, being economists, they started arguing: standard theory says more options can never make you worse off, since you can always just not eat the cashews. Yet they were glad to have the option removed. The episode captures **self-control**: a far-sighted 'planner' and a short-sighted 'doer' living in one head.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Removing an option can make people happier.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sometimes the best choice is to take the bowl away.

spotlights.name: The Cornell coffee mugs
spotlights.spot_it: Mugs handed to every other student, and owners who would not sell.
spotlights.story_md: Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Thaler gave Cornell students coffee mugs that sold for 6 dollars at the campus bookstore, to every other seat at random. Theory said about half the mugs should change hands, since they had landed with random people. In four markets, 11 trades were expected each time; only 1 to 4 happened. Owners asked a median 5.25 dollars; buyers offered under 3. A later run with 77 Simon Fraser students added 'choosers', picking between a mug and cash: sellers wanted 7.12 dollars, choosers 3.12, buyers 2.87. Owning a thing for minutes roughly doubled its value. This is the **endowment effect**, a direct consequence of loss aversion.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ownership itself changes value, which affects markets, law and trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hold the mug for five minutes and it costs double.

spotlights.name: Paying not to go to the gym
spotlights.spot_it: A gym membership that costs more per visit than buying day passes.
spotlights.story_md: Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier studied 7,752 members of three US health clubs over three years. Members on monthly contracts paid over 70 dollars a month and came about 4.3 times a month, so each visit cost them more than 17 dollars, when a 10-visit pass would have cost about 10 dollars a visit. They forwent roughly 600 dollars each over a membership. The authors' best explanation is overconfidence about future self-control: people sign up for the person they plan to be.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Present bias is a business model.
spotlights.memory_hook: You pay for the person you plan to become.

sections.title: Fairness, spite and the price of guilt
sections.intro_md:
Homo economicus is selfish by assumption. Real people care about fairness, reciprocity and what others will think, and they will give up money to enforce those norms. This was shown not with surveys but with **games played for real money** in laboratories, a method pioneered by Vernon Smith, who shared the 2002 Nobel with Kahneman.

These findings matter for policy because they show that money is not the only lever, and sometimes it is the wrong one. A price can crowd out a duty.

spotlights.name: The ultimatum game
spotlights.when: First run 1982, Werner Gueth and colleagues
spotlights.spot_it: One player splits a sum of money; the other can accept or destroy the whole thing.
spotlights.story_md: Player one gets, say, 100 rupees and proposes a split. Player two can accept, and both keep their shares, or reject, and both get nothing. Pure self-interest predicts the proposer offers 1 rupee and the responder takes it, since 1 beats 0. That almost never happens. Across thousands of runs, typical offers sit around 40 to 50 percent, and offers below about 20 percent are often rejected. People pay to punish what they see as an insult. Anthropologists later ran it in 15 small-scale societies: Peru's Machiguenga offered little, while some groups offered more than half. Fairness is universal; its level is cultural.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the cleanest proof that people trade money for fairness.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nothing for both of us beats an insult for me.

spotlights.name: The day-care fine that backfired
spotlights.spot_it: Parents fined for late pick-ups, who then came late more often.
spotlights.story_md: Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini watched 10 private day-care centres in Haifa for 20 weeks. After four weeks, six centres announced a fine of 10 shekels for parents who arrived more than 10 minutes late; four centres did nothing. Lateness at the fined centres rose steadily and settled at almost twice its old level. When the fine was removed in week 17, lateness stayed high. Before, lateness was a favour asked of teachers, policed by guilt. The fine turned it into a service anyone could buy, cheaply. Once the moral norm was gone, it did not come back.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Money can crowd out duty, permanently.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten shekels bought parents a clear conscience.

spotlights.name: Vernon Smith and the economics lab
spotlights.spot_it: An American economist who ran markets in classrooms, with students as buyers and sellers.
spotlights.story_md: In 1956, as a young teacher at Purdue, Vernon Smith split his class into buyers and sellers, gave each a secret value for an imaginary good, and let them trade. Prices converged on the textbook equilibrium with surprisingly few traders. Smith spent his career building **experimental economics**, testing auction designs and market rules in the lab before governments used them. He shared the 2002 Nobel with Kahneman. The pairing was telling: Smith's experiments often showed markets working better than expected, while Kahneman's showed individuals erring. Both used real money in controlled experiments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The lab experiment became a normal economist's tool.
spotlights.memory_hook: The classroom became a market, and the market worked.

sections.title: Nudge: steering without forbidding
sections.intro_md:
In 2008 Thaler and Cass Sunstein, a Chicago law professor, published **Nudge**. Its argument fits on a napkin. Every choice is presented in some way: a menu has an order, a form has a pre-ticked box, a cafeteria puts something at eye level. There is no neutral design, so the designer, whom they call the **choice architect**, may as well choose the arrangement that helps people by their own lights.

A nudge, in their definition, changes behaviour predictably without forbidding any option or significantly changing economic incentives. Putting fruit at eye level is a nudge. Banning junk food is not. They called the philosophy **libertarian paternalism**: paternalist because it steers, libertarian because you can always opt out.

The book landed as governments were broke after the 2008 crash and looking for cheap policies. Within two years, the UK and the US had nudge teams.

visual.title: Organ donation consent: opt-in versus opt-out (Johnson and Goldstein 2003, effective consent %)

spotlights.name: Nudge, the book
spotlights.spot_it: A yellow-covered bestseller by an economist and a law professor.
spotlights.story_md: Nudge argued that governments and firms should make the good choice the easy choice. Its examples became clichés: the urinal fly, cafeteria layout, automatic pension enrolment, organ donation defaults. Its definition is precise: a nudge must be cheap to avoid. The book became a bestseller and found fans across the political spectrum, from David Cameron's Conservatives to Barack Obama's White House, because it promised better outcomes without new taxes or bans.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave governments a cheap, politically easy toolkit.
spotlights.memory_hook: Make the good choice the easy choice.

spotlights.name: Do defaults save lives?
spotlights.spot_it: Neighbouring countries with near-identical cultures and wildly different donor rates.
spotlights.story_md: Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared European countries where you must tick a box to become an organ donor with countries where you are presumed willing unless you tick a box to refuse. Effective consent in opt-in Germany was about 12 percent; in culturally similar opt-out Austria it was 99.98 percent. Denmark, opt-in, about 4 percent; Sweden, opt-out, about 86 percent. The caution, often dropped: registered consent is not the same as organs transplanted. Families still decide at the bedside, and Spain's high rates owe much to its hospital system.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most quoted chart in behavioural policy.
spotlights.memory_hook: 12 percent in Germany, 99.98 in Austria: same people, different box.

spotlights.name: The piano stairs
spotlights.spot_it: A subway staircase painted like piano keys, each step playing a note.
spotlights.story_md: At Odenplan station in Stockholm, an advertising agency working for Volkswagen turned the stairs beside an escalator into a working keyboard. The video, part of a campaign called 'The Fun Theory', claimed 66 percent more people than normal chose the stairs. It has been watched tens of millions of times and appears in countless talks about nudging. Treat it as a brilliant advert, not a study: there was no control group, no published data and no follow-up on whether the effect lasted once the novelty wore off. It is still a good illustration of one design idea: make the healthy option more fun, not just more virtuous.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A famous example that is really marketing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fun beats virtue, at least on day one.

sections.title: Pensions: the biggest win
sections.intro_md:
If you ask what behavioural economics actually changed, the clearest answer is retirement saving, where the reward is decades away, the forms are dull and doing nothing is easy.

Three findings mattered. Automatic enrolment showed that inertia, the problem, could be the solution. Save More Tomorrow showed that people will commit their future pay rises to saving even when they will not cut today's spending. Sweden's 2000 pension reform showed what happens when you offer hundreds of funds and a default.

The ideas went into law: the US Pension Protection Act of 2006 made auto-enrolment easier for employers, and the SECURE 2.0 Act requires most new 401(k) plans from 2025 to enrol workers automatically at 3 to 10 percent of pay, rising 1 point a year. The UK went further, making auto-enrolment compulsory for employers from 2012.

visual.title: UK eligible employees saving in a workplace pension (%)

spotlights.name: The power of suggestion
spotlights.spot_it: One company switches from 'opt in' to 'opt out', and participation leaps.
spotlights.story_md: Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied a large US company that changed its 401(k) savings plan in 1998: new hires were enrolled automatically unless they said no. For employees hired under auto-enrolment, participation was about 86 percent. For comparable employees hired before, it had been 37 percent at the same stage. The catch was just as revealing: most auto-enrolled workers stayed at the default contribution rate of 3 percent and the default money-market fund, even if they would have chosen more on their own. Defaults cut both ways.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The paper that launched auto-enrolment worldwide.
spotlights.memory_hook: 37 percent opted in; 86 percent did not opt out.

spotlights.name: Save More Tomorrow
spotlights.spot_it: Workers commit now to raise their saving rate at each future pay rise.
spotlights.story_md: Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed a plan that uses three biases against themselves. People hate cutting take-home pay (loss aversion), so contributions rise only when pay rises. People are generous with their future selves (present bias), so they sign up now for increases later. And people stick with what they set up (inertia), so the increases keep happening. At the first firm to try it, participants' saving rates went from 3.5 percent to 13.6 percent of pay over four pay rises. The evidence came from one company with no randomised control, but automatic escalation is now built into US law and many plans.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned three weaknesses into a savings machine.
spotlights.memory_hook: Promise your raise, not your rupee.

spotlights.name: UK automatic enrolment
spotlights.spot_it: Every UK employer must enrol eligible workers in a pension; workers may opt out.
spotlights.story_md: The Pensions Commission led by Adair Turner recommended in 2005 that employers enrol workers automatically, and the Pensions Act 2008 made it law. From October 2012, starting with the largest employers, workers aged 22 and over earning above a threshold were put into a workplace pension with employer contributions, now 8 percent of qualifying earnings in total. Participation among eligible employees rose from 55 percent in 2012 to 88 percent in 2020 and about 90 percent in 2025, or 22.6 million savers. Among 22 to 29 year olds it rose by about 50 points, to 85 percent, between 2012 and 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Probably the largest behavioural policy ever run.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten million new savers, by doing nothing.

spotlights.name: Sweden's pension smorgasbord
spotlights.spot_it: A national pension menu with 456 funds and a heavily advertised push to pick your own.
spotlights.story_md: In 2000 Sweden let every worker invest part of their public pension in a fund of their choice, from a catalogue of 456 funds, backed by advertising urging people to choose. A default fund existed for those who did nothing. Henrik Cronqvist and Thaler found the active choosers did worse: they piled into recent winners, home-country stocks and the fund they knew, especially a technology fund that crashed after the dot-com peak. In later years fewer than 10 percent of new entrants chose at all. Thaler's lesson: if you offer a default, design it well, because most people will end up in it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: More choice is not automatically better.
spotlights.memory_hook: 456 funds, and the default won.

sections.title: Nudge units inside government
sections.intro_md:
In July 2010 the new UK coalition government set up a seven-person team in the Cabinet Office, officially the Behavioural Insights Team, universally the 'Nudge Unit'. It had a sunset clause: shut down in two years unless it saved at least ten times its cost. It survived.

The US followed with the Social and Behavioral Sciences Team in 2014, formalised by Barack Obama's Executive Order 13707 in September 2015. The OECD has now mapped more than 300 institutions applying behavioural science to policy in 63 countries.

The signature method is not the nudge itself but the **randomised trial**: send half the letters one way and half the other, and measure. That habit may be the field's most durable legacy.

visual.title: Where the ideas went to work

pins.label: Wales: first UK opt-out organ law

spotlights.name: The Behavioural Insights Team
spotlights.spot_it: A small team of civil servants and psychologists that began in 10 Downing Street's orbit.
spotlights.story_md: Led by the psychologist David Halpern, the team started with seven people and a deadline. Its early wins were small and measurable: rewording tax letters and sending court-fine reminders by text, each tested with randomised trials, and its 2012 sunset review credited it with savings of about 22 times its cost. In February 2014 it was spun out of the Cabinet Office as a 'social purpose company', a third each owned by government, Nesta and staff, with Nesta providing 1.9 million pounds; it later became wholly owned by Nesta.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The model every later nudge unit copied.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven people, two years to prove themselves.

spotlights.name: 'Nine out of ten people pay on time'
spotlights.spot_it: A tax reminder letter with one extra sentence about what neighbours do.
spotlights.story_md: Working with HM Revenue and Customs, the team added a line to reminder letters for people late with their tax: most people in your area pay on time. Field experiments covering more than 200,000 taxpayers found that **descriptive social norms**, telling people what others actually do, raised payment rates, and that the more local and specific the norm, the stronger the effect. Messages about what taxes pay for also helped. Reported effects vary by trial and outcome, from a couple of percentage points to about 15 points for the best letter in the early pilot, with millions of pounds collected sooner at almost no cost.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Social norms are cheap and they move money.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your neighbours paid. Have you?

spotlights.name: Opt-out organ donation in the UK
spotlights.spot_it: Laws that treat adults as willing donors unless they register a refusal.
spotlights.story_md: Wales was first in the UK, moving to 'deemed consent' in December 2015. England followed on 20 May 2020 with the Organ Donation (Deemed Consent) Act, known as Max and Keira's Law after a boy who received a heart and the girl who donated it, and Scotland in 2021. Families are still consulted. The honest result: consent rates rose, but total donations depend heavily on hospital systems, family conversations and intensive care capacity. Defaults change who is asked and how; they do not by themselves create organs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A nudge written into law.
spotlights.memory_hook: Max got a heart; Keira gave it; the law took both their names.

sections.title: Money, markets and bubbles
sections.intro_md:
Financial economics was the stronghold of rationality. The efficient market hypothesis, associated with Eugene Fama, says prices reflect all available information, so you cannot reliably beat the market. Behavioural finance agreed that beating the market is hard, but argued that prices can still be wrong for long periods, with bubbles, excess volatility, and investors who sell winners too early and cling to losers.

The 2013 Nobel captured the standoff: it was shared by Fama, the champion of efficient markets, and Robert Shiller, its sharpest critic.

This matters beyond Wall Street. India's derivatives boom of the 2020s, in which nine in ten individual traders lost money year after year, is a live behavioural finance case: overconfidence, the lottery-like appeal of options, and the pull of a few big wins.

spotlights.name: Robert Shiller and Irrational Exuberance
spotlights.spot_it: A Yale economist who called two bubbles in a row, stocks in 2000 and housing in 2005.
spotlights.story_md: On 5 December 1996, Fed chairman Alan Greenspan asked in a speech how we know when 'irrational exuberance' has inflated asset prices. Robert Shiller had testified to the Fed days earlier. He used the phrase as the title of a book published in March 2000, the very month the dot-com boom peaked, arguing with his long-run price-to-earnings measure that stocks were wildly overvalued. They crashed. The 2005 second edition warned about house prices, before the 2007 to 2008 collapse. In 2013 Shiller shared the Nobel 'for their empirical analysis of asset prices' with Eugene Fama and Lars Peter Hansen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made 'bubble' a respectable word in economics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two crashes, called in advance, in one book's two editions.

spotlights.name: Why stocks pay so much more than bonds
spotlights.spot_it: Investors who check their portfolios often feel every dip, and demand a higher reward.
spotlights.story_md: Over the 20th century, US stocks returned several percentage points a year more than safe bonds, more than standard models of risk could explain: the 'equity premium puzzle'. Benartzi and Thaler proposed **myopic loss aversion**. Investors feel losses about twice as strongly as gains, and they look at their accounts often. Stocks fall in many short periods even when they rise over decades, so a frequent checker experiences lots of painful losses. Their simulations found the premium matched prospect theory if investors evaluated portfolios about once a year. Practical advice: check less.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links a big market fact to a simple human habit.
spotlights.memory_hook: Check yearly, sleep better, hold more stocks.

spotlights.name: India's options boom and SEBI's numbers

where.label: SEBI Bhavan, Bandra Kurla Complex, Mumbai

spotlights.spot_it: A pop-up on every Indian trading app: '9 out of 10 individual traders in equity F&O incurred net losses'.
spotlights.story_md: From 2023 SEBI required brokers to show a risk disclosure, covering at least half the screen, when clients log in: nine in ten individual F&O traders lose money. Losses kept growing anyway. SEBI's July 2025 study found 91 percent of individual traders lost money in FY25. After rules raising lot sizes and limiting weekly expiries, its FY26 study, reported in August 2026, found individual traders' net losses fell 18 percent to about 91,685 crore rupees, from a revised 1.12 lakh crore, and the share of loss-makers to 87.7 percent. Before trading costs, 82.1 percent lost; costs alone pushed about 4.4 lakh traders from profit into loss.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A behavioural warning was not enough; structural rules moved the numbers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine in ten lose, and the pop-up says so every login.

sections.title: Business, apps and dark patterns
sections.intro_md:
Companies used behavioural insight long before academics named it.

What the field added was measurement, and with it a new problem. Digital products can run thousands of experiments a week, testing which button colour, wording or default makes people click. The same tools that help people save can help a company make cancelling hard. In 2010 the designer Harry Brignull coined the term **dark patterns** for interfaces that trick users: pre-ticked boxes, hidden costs, 'confirmshaming' ('No thanks, I don't like saving money') and subscription traps. Thaler calls the harmful version 'sludge'.

Regulators have caught up. The EU's Digital Services Act bans dark patterns on online platforms, India's consumer authority listed 13 banned types in 2023, and in September 2025 the US Federal Trade Commission extracted 2.5 billion dollars from Amazon over Prime sign-ups and cancellations.

Must buy or sign up to something else
Easy to join, hard to cancel
Design that hides the option you want
Advertised offer swapped at the end
Repeated prompts until you give in
Silent charges after a free trial

spotlights.name: The energy report with a smiley face
spotlights.spot_it: A utility letter comparing your electricity use with about 100 neighbours.
spotlights.story_md: The company Opower sent households a home energy report showing their use against similar nearby homes, with one or two smiley faces for doing well. Hunt Allcott's analysis of a randomised trial with about 80,000 Minnesota households found the reports cut energy use by about 2 percent. Across more than 110 US utilities the effect was 1 to 3 percent, and it persisted: households that stopped receiving reports after two years kept saving about 2 percent. At one site in India, reports cut electricity use by 7 percent over four months. Two percent sounds small; across millions of homes it is a power plant's worth of electricity, bought with letters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Social comparison works at national scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: A smiley face on a power bill saves 2 percent.

spotlights.name: Dark patterns
spotlights.spot_it: A cancel button in pale grey text, a pre-ticked insurance box, a countdown that resets when you reload.
spotlights.story_md: Harry Brignull, a British user-experience designer, registered darkpatterns.org in 2010 to name and shame tricks built into websites and apps. The categories read like a behavioural economics syllabus run in reverse: sneaky defaults, fake countdowns, 'only 3 left', and cancellation mazes. Thaler and Sunstein insist that a real nudge must be transparent and easy to avoid, and in the user's interest; a dark pattern fails all three. Regulators in the EU, US and India now use the term in law, so a designer's coinage has become a legal category.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The same science can help or exploit.
spotlights.memory_hook: A nudge holds the door; a dark pattern hides it.

spotlights.name: Amazon's 2.5 billion dollar Prime settlement
spotlights.spot_it: A settlement the US Federal Trade Commission called historic, over sign-up and cancel screens.
spotlights.story_md: The FTC sued Amazon in 2023, alleging that it steered shoppers into Prime subscriptions with confusing buttons and made cancelling deliberately hard through a four-page, six-click process that, the FTC said, Amazon staff called the 'Iliad Flow', after Homer's epic. On 25 September 2025, days into the Seattle trial, Amazon agreed to pay a 1 billion dollar civil penalty and 1.5 billion dollars in refunds to roughly 35 million customers, up to 51 dollars each, and to make cancelling simple. Amazon admitted no wrongdoing. For behavioural economists it was a milestone: an interface, not a price, was treated as the harm.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Choice architecture can now cost billions in court.
spotlights.memory_hook: An epic called Iliad, for leaving Prime.

sections.title: The India chapter
sections.intro_md:
India has been both a laboratory and an adopter. Some of the field's most cited experiments ran in Indian villages, and the state has used behavioural ideas at scale, sometimes without the label.

The official turn came in July 2019, when the Economic Survey, written under Chief Economic Adviser Krishnamurthy Subramanian, devoted Chapter 2 to 'Policy for Homo Sapiens, Not Homo Economicus'. It credited Swachh Bharat and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao with using social norms, and proposed a nudge unit. NITI Aayog set up a Behavioural Insights Unit later that year with the Gates Foundation and Ashoka University's Centre for Social and Behaviour Change.

Since then the vocabulary has spread: SEBI's loss warnings, the consumer regulator's dark-pattern rules, the Income Tax Department's NUDGE campaigns, and NITI Aayog's vice-chair calling in August 2026 for 'behavioural audits' of schemes.

pins.label: Tamil Nadu: sugarcane farmers and scarcity
New Delhi: Economic Survey and NITI Aayog unit

spotlights.name: 'Policy for Homo Sapiens, Not Homo Economicus'
spotlights.spot_it: A chapter of India's annual Economic Survey that reads like a nudge manifesto.
spotlights.story_md: The chapter argued that Indians, like everyone, respond to social norms, defaults and repetition, and that policy should use them. It listed three principles: emphasise beneficial social norms, change default options, and reinforce repeatedly. It proposed moving 'from Beti Bachao Beti Padhao to BADLAV', 'from Swachh Bharat to Sundar Bharat', from 'Give it up' to 'Think about the subsidy' for LPG, and from tax evasion to tax compliance. Its most debated suggestion was invoking the 'pious obligation' doctrine, the religious duty to repay debts, to discourage wilful default. Whatever its merits, it made 'nudge' part of Indian policy language.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's government formally adopted the behavioural lens.
spotlights.memory_hook: Homo sapiens, not Homo economicus.

spotlights.name: Give It Up: asking the rich to drop their gas subsidy
spotlights.spot_it: A campaign asking better-off households to surrender their LPG cylinder subsidy voluntarily.
spotlights.story_md: In March 2015 Prime Minister Narendra Modi appealed to households that could afford it to give up their cooking gas subsidy, with the savings going to connect poor households. It was a pure appeal to public spirit. Uptake started slowly, with about 5.5 lakh of 15.3 crore consumers by June 2015, then accelerated as the campaign was pushed through distributors and SMS, with the promise that each surrendered subsidy would fund a gas connection for a poor household. By April 2016 the count passed one crore. The 2019 Economic Survey cited it as a model and proposed a sharper 'Think about the subsidy' default.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Voluntary appeals can work when giving is made visible.
spotlights.memory_hook: One crore households said 'keep it'.

spotlights.name: A kilo of lentils for a vaccination
spotlights.spot_it: Village immunisation camps where mothers received dal and steel plates.
spotlights.story_md: In rural Udaipur, Rajasthan, only a small share of children were fully immunised, even where vaccines were free. Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, Rachel Glennerster and Dhruva Kothari, working with the NGO Seva Mandir, compared villages with reliable monthly camps, camps plus a 1 kg bag of lentils per shot and a set of plates on completion, and controls. Full immunisation reached 39 percent with camps plus lentils, 18 percent with camps alone and 6 percent in control villages. The incentive halved the cost per fully immunised child, to about 28 dollars, because nurses were no longer idle. Small rewards overcame procrastination where the benefit was invisible and delayed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tiny, immediate rewards beat distant, invisible benefits.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six percent, 18 percent, 39 percent: the dal did the rest.

spotlights.name: Scarcity and the sugarcane farmers

where.label: Villupuram and Tiruvannamalai area, Tamil Nadu

spotlights.spot_it: The same farmers tested before harvest, when broke, and after, when paid.
spotlights.story_md: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir argued in their book Scarcity (2013) that being short of money taxes the mind, using up 'bandwidth'. With Anandi Mani and Jiaying Zhao they tested it on 464 sugarcane farmers in Tamil Nadu, who get most of their income in one annual payment. The same farmers scored worse on fluid-intelligence and attention tests before harvest, when money was tight, than after. Time, nutrition and work effort did not explain it, nor did stress. The gap was comparable to losing a night's sleep. Implication: poor people do not make worse decisions because of who they are, but because of what scarcity does to anyone.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Poverty is a cognitive tax, not a character flaw.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same farmer, smarter after payday.

spotlights.name: Swachh Bharat and 'Darwaza Band'
spotlights.spot_it: Celebrity adverts telling villagers to shut the door on open defecation.
spotlights.story_md: India's Swachh Bharat Mission, launched on 2 October 2014, reported more than 10 crore rural household toilets built by October 2019. Officials knew from earlier programmes that building toilets did not guarantee use, so the mission paired construction with behaviour change: village 'triggering' meetings that made open defecation shameful, local volunteers called swachhagrahis, and the 'Darwaza Band' (close the door) campaign with Amitabh Bachchan and Anushka Sharma, aimed at men, the last to adopt latrines. India declared itself open defecation free in October 2019. Independent surveys found real gains but also continued open defecation in several states, so the scale of usage remains debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest norm-change campaign the field can point to.
spotlights.memory_hook: Build the toilet, then shut the door on the old habit.

spotlights.name: Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo
spotlights.spot_it: A Kolkata-raised economist and his French co-author and wife, founders of J-PAL at MIT.
spotlights.story_md: Banerjee grew up in Kolkata, studied at Presidency College and JNU, and with Duflo and Michael Kremer won the 2019 economics Nobel 'for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty'. They are not behavioural economists in the narrow sense, but their randomised trials in India and elsewhere kept running into behavioural facts: people delay vaccinating, fail to buy cheap fertiliser after harvest, and respond to small immediate rewards. J-PAL, which they founded in 2003, now runs or supports trials worldwide, many in India, with governments as partners.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They brought the field's tools to India's villages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Randomise first, then argue.

spotlights.name: The taxman's NUDGE
spotlights.spot_it: SMS and email asking taxpayers to recheck their returns, before any notice is sent.
spotlights.story_md: The Income Tax Department named its approach NUDGE, Non-intrusive Usage of Data to Guide and Enable. Using data received from abroad under automatic exchange agreements, it messaged taxpayers whose returns seemed to omit foreign assets, inviting them to correct the return themselves. In the first campaign, from 17 November 2024, 24,678 taxpayers revised their returns and disclosed foreign assets worth about 29,208 crore rupees. A second round began on 28 November 2025. The Economic Survey 2025-26, in January 2026, credited such nudges with better collection and less litigation. It is the UK tax-letter idea, with Indian data infrastructure behind it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder before a notice keeps cases out of court.
spotlights.memory_hook: A polite SMS that found 29,000 crore.

sections.title: Cracks: replication, fraud and critics
sections.intro_md:
From about 2011, psychology went through a **replication crisis**. Large coordinated efforts re-ran famous studies and many did not hold up. The core of prospect theory, loss aversion, defaults and present bias has replicated well. Many cute 'priming' and 'choice overload' effects have not.

Then came fraud. In 2021 the blog Data Colada showed that a famous field study on honesty, co-authored by Dan Ariely and Francesca Gino, used fabricated data. In 2023 the same bloggers flagged further problems in Gino's work; Harvard investigated, and in May 2025 revoked her tenure.

A third blow was statistical. Across every trial two US nudge units ran, published or not, the average effect was about a sixth of what journals reported. Critics go further: Gerd Gigerenzer argues people's shortcuts are often smart, and Nick Chater and George Loewenstein argue that nudging individuals let governments dodge harder structural reforms.

visual.title: Average nudge effect: published papers versus everything two nudge units ran

spotlights.name: The jam study
spotlights.spot_it: A tasting table with 24 jams versus 6, and the claim that fewer choices sold more.
spotlights.story_md: Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth in an upmarket California supermarket, alternating between 24 and 6 flavours of jam. More shoppers stopped at the big display, but only about 3 percent of them later bought a jar, against about 30 percent at the small one. 'Choice overload' became a management mantra. Then Benjamin Scheibehenne tried to replicate it and found nothing. His 2010 meta-analysis of the literature found an average choice-overload effect of nearly zero, with large effects in some settings and reversals in others. The careful conclusion: too much choice sometimes hurts, especially when preferences are unclear, but it is not a law.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A famous result that shrank on inspection.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-four jams, and an effect that mostly vanished.

spotlights.name: The odometer study and the fake data
spotlights.spot_it: An honesty study where signing at the top of a form supposedly reduced lying.
spotlights.story_md: A 2012 paper in PNAS by Lisa Shu, Nina Mazar, Francesca Gino, Max Bazerman and Dan Ariely reported that people were more honest when they signed an honesty pledge at the top of a form rather than the bottom. Its headline field study used car-insurance customers reporting their odometer readings, 13,488 of them. In August 2021 Data Colada showed the mileage data were fabricated, with statistical signatures no real data would have. The paper was retracted. Ariely, who supplied the data file, said he did not fabricate it and did not know who did.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A behavioural policy built on fake data spread before anyone checked.
spotlights.memory_hook: The study on honesty was the dishonest one.

spotlights.name: Harvard revokes Francesca Gino's tenure
spotlights.spot_it: The first known removal of a tenured Harvard professor since the rules were formalised in the 1940s.
spotlights.story_md: Francesca Gino, a Harvard Business School professor who studied dishonesty, was placed on unpaid leave in June 2023 after Data Colada flagged suspected data manipulation in four of her papers and an internal investigation found research misconduct. She denied it and sued Harvard and the bloggers for 25 million dollars; a judge dismissed the defamation claims against Data Colada in 2024 while letting contract claims against Harvard proceed. In May 2025 the Harvard Corporation revoked her tenure, which no one could recall happening since at least the 1940s. The case, with Ariely's, made 'dishonesty researchers accused of dishonesty' the field's most damaging headline.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It forced the field to take data checks seriously.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tenure revoked: first time in about 80 years.

spotlights.name: The shrinking nudge
spotlights.spot_it: Every trial two nudge units ran, compared with the trials that got published.
spotlights.story_md: Stefano DellaVigna and Elizabeth Linos gained access to all 126 randomised trials run by two large US nudge units, covering about 23 million people, including the ones nobody published. The average nudge raised take-up by 1.4 percentage points, an 8 percent increase. Nudges published in academic journals reported 8.7 points, a 33 percent increase. About 70 percent of the gap came from selective publication of small, lucky studies. Separately, a 2022 re-analysis of a large nudge meta-analysis found no clear overall effect after correcting for publication bias. The fair summary: nudges usually work, modestly, and are cheap; they are not magic.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It recalibrated what governments can expect.
spotlights.memory_hook: Journals said 33 percent. Reality said 8.

spotlights.name: The hot hand that came back
spotlights.spot_it: A basketball player on a streak, and an argument about whether streaks are real.
spotlights.story_md: In 1985 Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky studied basketball shooting and found no evidence that a player who has just made several shots is more likely to make the next. Fans and players who believed in the 'hot hand' were, it seemed, seeing patterns in randomness. For 30 years it was a favourite example of human error. Then in 2018 Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed that the standard way of measuring streaks in finite sequences is biased against finding them. Correcting the bias reversed the original conclusion: modest hot hands do exist. The field's own experts had committed a statistical error about statistical errors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Experts can be biased about bias.
spotlights.memory_hook: The fallacy was the fallacy.

spotlights.name: Gerd Gigerenzer, the loyal opposition

where.label: Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Berlin

spotlights.spot_it: A German psychologist who argues that simple rules of thumb are often smarter than complex models.
spotlights.story_md: Gigerenzer, long a director at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, has argued since the 1990s that the heuristics-and-biases school sets people up to fail with artificial puzzles. In the real world, he says, simple heuristics are often **ecologically rational**: fast and accurate in the environments they evolved for. Rewrite probability problems as natural frequencies ('10 out of 1,000 women') instead of percentages and most people, doctors included, get them right. His policy alternative to nudging is **boosting**: teach people skills such as reading risk, rather than steering them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the strongest scientific challenge to the 'humans are biased' story.
spotlights.memory_hook: Do not nudge people. Boost them.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Behavioural economics is unusually prone to myths, because its findings make good stories and good stories travel faster than corrections. Some numbers in circulation were never measured (the 80 percent fly). Some came from studies that later shrank (choice overload, many priming effects) or were faked (the honesty pledge).

There is also a myth about the field itself: that it proved humans are 'irrational'. Most researchers avoid that word. The claim is narrower. People deviate from one particular model of rationality in predictable directions, and those deviations are often sensible given limited time and attention. Loss aversion is itself under debate: a few researchers argue it is weaker or context-dependent, but the 2024 meta-analysis of 607 estimates still puts the average near 2.

data.claim: The urinal fly cut spillage by 80 percent
data.verdict: Unmeasured. Manager's estimate; others say about 50 percent.
Overstated. People deviate predictably from one model.

data.claim: Losses hurt about twice as much as gains
data.verdict: Holds on average (about 1.96), varies by person and context.

data.claim: Opt-out laws massively raise organ donation
data.verdict: Consent rises; actual transplants depend on hospitals and families.

data.claim: Too much choice stops people buying
data.verdict: Average effect near zero across studies; sometimes true.
Drop it. The key field data were fabricated; lab results did not replicate.

data.claim: The hot hand is a fallacy
data.verdict: Reversed in 2018: small hot hands exist.

data.claim: Willpower is a muscle that tires (ego depletion)
data.verdict: A 23-lab replication found an effect near zero.
Average at scale about 1.4 percentage points; cheap but modest.

spotlights.name: Ego depletion: the willpower muscle
spotlights.spot_it: The idea that resisting one temptation leaves you weaker against the next.
spotlights.story_md: In 1998 Roy Baumeister's lab reported that people who resisted freshly baked cookies and ate radishes instead gave up sooner on a later unsolvable puzzle. Self-control, the theory went, is a limited resource, like a muscle that tires; some follow-ups even suggested a sugary drink restored it. Hundreds of studies followed and the idea reached self-help shelves and policy talk about decision fatigue. In 2016 a pre-registered replication across 23 laboratories and 2,141 participants found an effect indistinguishable from zero. Baumeister disputed the test. Many researchers now treat ego depletion as unproven, a warning for any nudge built on it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A pillar of self-control thinking that may not exist.
spotlights.memory_hook: Radishes, cookies and an effect that vanished in 23 labs.

sections.title: What is happening now (2024 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The field is in a sober middle age. Its founders are passing: Kahneman died in March 2024. Its fraud cases have reached courts and tenure committees. Its effect sizes have been cut down to size. Yet its ideas are more embedded in law and regulation than ever.

The direction of travel has shifted from nudging individuals to regulating the people who design choices: platforms, brokers and subscription businesses. There are also calls, such as Chater and Loewenstein's, to pair nudges with structural rules like taxes and mandates.

In India, 2025 and 2026 brought a cluster of behavioural moves: the CCPA's dark-pattern self-audit order, the Income Tax Department's second NUDGE round, an Economic Survey that praised nudges in tax, SEBI's new F&O loss data, and the first national nudge awards.

spotlights.name: Kahneman's last decision
spotlights.spot_it: A Nobel laureate in decision-making who decided, at 90 and still active, how to end his life.
spotlights.story_md: Princeton announced in March 2024 that Kahneman had died peacefully, 22 days after his 90th birthday. A year later the Wall Street Journal's Jason Zweig, a friend who had worked with him on Thinking, Fast and Slow, revealed that Kahneman had ended his life at an assisted-dying facility in Switzerland. He was still working; in emails to close friends he explained that he expected decline and preferred to leave before it came. The essay set off wide debate. For readers of his work it carried an echo of the peak-end rule he described: how an experience ends shapes how it is remembered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The field's founder applied its questions to his own death.
spotlights.memory_hook: He chose the ending his research said we remember.

sections.title: The best facts
sections.intro_md:
Five to keep. A psychologist who never took an economics course won the economics Nobel. A fine made Haifa parents later, and they stayed late after it was scrapped. A decision theorist leaked the Pentagon Papers. A famous study of honesty used fake data. In Udaipur, a kilo of dal per shot raised full immunisation from 6 to 39 percent.

The full scored list, with a source for every item, is in the best facts panel.

sections.title: Recap: what it changed, and what it did not
sections.intro_md:
**What it found.** People judge outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point, and losses weigh about twice as much. Defaults stick, irrelevant numbers anchor, plans assume the best case and the present beats the future. People pay to punish unfairness, and money can crowd out duty.

**What it changed.** Pensions above all: auto-enrolment and escalation now cover tens of millions of savers. Tax letters, organ-donation laws, energy bills, a habit of testing policy with randomised trials, and consumer law that treats manipulative design as harm.

**What it did not.** It did not prove people irrational. Many famous effects shrank or vanished, and fabricated data hit two star researchers. Nudges at scale are real but small.

**India.** Udaipur and Tamil Nadu experiments, the 2019 Economic Survey, SEBI warnings, banned dark patterns and the taxman's NUDGE.

**One line.** Behavioural economics did not overthrow economics. It made it describe humans.

cards.front: Who is this psychologist, and what prize did he win in 2002?
cards.back: Daniel Kahneman. The economics Nobel, for bringing psychology into economics.

cards.front: Who is this economist, and for what did he win the 2017 Nobel?
cards.back: Richard Thaler, for his contributions to behavioural economics.

cards.front: What is loss aversion, and roughly how strong is it?
cards.back: Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good. Best estimate: about 1.96 times (2024 meta-analysis of 607 estimates).

cards.front: Prospect theory was published in the journal ____ in 1979.
cards.back: Econometrica. It is the journal's most cited paper.

cards.front: In the rigged-wheel experiment, what did people guess after seeing 10, and after 65?
cards.back: Median guesses of 25 percent and 45 percent for African countries in the UN. That is anchoring.

cards.front: Why can 'Linda is a bank teller and a feminist' never be more likely than 'Linda is a bank teller'?
cards.back: Because every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller. Adding a condition can only shrink the probability. Choosing it is the conjunction fallacy.

cards.front: Asian disease problem: what share chose the sure option when framed as lives saved, and the gamble when framed as deaths?
cards.back: 72 percent chose the sure option in the 'saved' frame; 78 percent chose the gamble in the 'die' frame.

cards.front: This building's budget rose from about A$7 million to A$102 million. Name it and the bias.
cards.back: The Sydney Opera House, the textbook case of the planning fallacy.

cards.front: In the 1990 mug experiment with sellers, buyers and choosers, what were the median valuations?
cards.back: Sellers 7.12 dollars, choosers 3.12, buyers 2.87: the endowment effect.

cards.front: What happened when Haifa day-care centres fined parents for picking up late?
cards.back: Lateness rose to almost twice its old level, and stayed high after the fine was removed. A fine became a price.

cards.front: In the ultimatum game, what does pure self-interest predict, and what happens?
cards.back: Predicts the tiniest offer, always accepted. In practice offers average 40 to 50 percent and offers below about 20 percent are often rejected.

cards.front: A nudge changes behaviour without forbidding options or significantly changing ____.
cards.back: Economic incentives (Thaler and Sunstein's definition).

cards.front: Organ donation consent: Germany (opt-in) versus Austria (opt-out)?
cards.back: About 12 percent versus 99.98 percent in Johnson and Goldstein's 2003 data.

cards.front: Madrian and Shea: 401(k) participation before and after automatic enrolment?
cards.back: About 37 percent for earlier hires at the same stage versus about 86 percent for auto-enrolled hires.

cards.front: Save More Tomorrow: what happened to participants' saving rates?
cards.back: From 3.5 percent to 13.6 percent of pay over four pay rises.

cards.front: When was the UK Behavioural Insights Team created, and how big was it?
cards.back: July 2010, seven people, with a two-year sunset clause.

cards.front: Average nudge effect: published papers versus all trials of two US nudge units?
cards.back: 8.7 percentage points (33 percent) in journals versus 1.4 points (8 percent) at scale.

cards.front: Udaipur immunisation trial: full immunisation in control, camps, and camps plus lentils?
cards.back: 6 percent, 18 percent and 39 percent.

cards.front: Which Indian document carried the chapter 'Policy for Homo Sapiens, Not Homo Economicus'?
cards.back: The Economic Survey 2018-19 (July 2019), Volume 1, Chapter 2.

cards.front: What did SEBI's FY26 study find about individual F&O traders?
cards.back: 87.7 percent lost money; total net losses about 91,685 crore rupees.

cards.front: This man gave his name to a paradox about unknown odds. What else is he famous for?
cards.back: Daniel Ellsberg. He leaked the Pentagon Papers in 1971.

cards.front: Name this polymath and the word he coined for choosing 'good enough'.
cards.back: Herbert Simon: satisficing. Nobel 1978.

cards.front: Whose 1759 book described loss aversion long before prospect theory?
cards.back: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments.

cards.front: This economist's 1936 phrase describes confidence driving investment. What is it?
cards.back: John Maynard Keynes: 'animal spirits'.

cards.front: Which aircraft gave its name to the sunk cost fallacy?
cards.back: Concorde: the 'Concorde fallacy'.

cards.front: What is etched into this urinal, and what number is falsely attached to it?
cards.back: A fly. The claimed 80 percent cut in spillage was never measured.

cards.front: Which story about self-control starts with this snack?
cards.back: Thaler's cashews: guests were grateful when he took the bowl away.

cards.front: Who is this co-author of Nudge, and which White House office did he run?
cards.back: Cass Sunstein, the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, 2009 to 2012.

cards.front: Who is this Yale economist, and which bubble did his March 2000 book call?
cards.back: Robert Shiller; the dot-com bubble, in Irrational Exuberance.

cards.front: Who is this Kolkata-raised Nobel laureate, and what was his 2019 prize for?
cards.back: Abhijit Banerjee, for an experimental approach to alleviating global poverty, shared with Duflo and Kremer.

cards.front: Who coined 'dark patterns' in 2010?
cards.back: Harry Brignull, a British user-experience designer.

cards.front: This German psychologist argues for 'boosting' rather than nudging. Who is he?
cards.back: Gerd Gigerenzer.

cards.front: What does the gym study show about monthly members?
cards.back: They paid over 17 dollars a visit when 10-visit passes cost 10: overconfidence about future self-control.

cards.front: Name Thaler's four contributions cited by the Nobel committee.
cards.back: Mental accounting, the endowment effect (limited rationality), social preferences (fairness), and self-control.

cards.front: What did the 2016 23-lab replication find about ego depletion?
cards.back: An effect indistinguishable from zero (d about 0.04).

cards.front: What did Miller and Sanjurjo show in 2018 about the hot hand?
cards.back: The standard streak measure was biased; corrected, the data show a real if modest hot hand.

cards.front: Why was the 2012 'sign at the top' honesty paper retracted?
cards.back: Its car-insurance odometer data were shown to be fabricated (Data Colada, 2021).

cards.front: What did Harvard do to Francesca Gino in May 2025?
cards.back: Revoked her tenure, the first such case there in about 80 years.

cards.front: What did Amazon agree to pay the FTC in September 2025?
cards.back: 2.5 billion dollars: a 1 billion penalty and 1.5 billion in refunds over Prime sign-up and cancellation design.

cards.front: How many dark patterns does India's 2023 CCPA guideline list?
cards.back: 13, from false urgency to subscription traps.

cards.front: The Income Tax Department's NUDGE stands for Non-intrusive Usage of Data to ____ and Enable.
cards.back: Guide.

cards.front: What did the scarcity study find among Tamil Nadu sugarcane farmers?
cards.back: The same farmers scored worse on cognitive tests before harvest, when short of money, than after.

cards.front: How did UK workplace pension participation change after auto-enrolment?
cards.back: From 55 percent of eligible employees in 2012 to 88 percent in 2020 and about 90 percent in 2025.

cards.front: What did Opower's neighbour-comparison letters do to energy use?
cards.back: Cut it by about 2 percent (1 to 3 percent across 110+ utilities).

cards.front: Why do frequent portfolio checkers demand higher returns from stocks (myopic loss aversion)?
cards.back: Short periods often show losses, and losses hurt about twice as much as gains please, so frequent checking makes stocks feel riskier.

cards.front: What was the Allais paradox's key lesson?
cards.back: Certainty carries a special premium: people violate expected utility when a sure thing is on offer (the certainty effect).

cards.front: When did Wales and England move to opt-out organ donation?
cards.back: Wales December 2015; England 20 May 2020 (Max and Keira's Law); Scotland 2021.

cards.front: What did the jam study claim, and what did the meta-analysis find?
cards.back: 3 percent bought from 24 jams versus 30 percent from 6; across studies the average choice-overload effect was near zero.

cards.front: What did Sweden's 2000 pension reform teach about choice?
cards.back: With 456 funds, active choosers did worse than the default fund; later almost everyone used the default.

cards.front: How did Kahneman die, and when did the manner become public?
cards.back: Assisted death in Switzerland on 27 March 2024; revealed in a WSJ essay in March 2025.

cards.front: Side dish: what did Ulysses do to resist the Sirens?
cards.back: Had his crew plug their ears with wax and tie him to the mast: a commitment device.

cards.front: Side dish: what is a commitment device?
cards.back: A choice made now that limits your future options, to protect long-term goals from short-term temptation.
