best_facts.fact: Daniel Kahneman won the 2002 economics Nobel without ever having taken an economics course: he was a psychologist.
best_facts.why_surprising: The top prize in economics went to an outsider.

best_facts.fact: Fining Haifa parents 10 shekels for late pick-ups almost doubled lateness, and it stayed high after the fine was scrapped.
best_facts.why_surprising: Punishment increased the behaviour it targeted.

best_facts.fact: Daniel Ellsberg, whose 1961 paradox founded the study of ambiguity aversion, is the same man who leaked the Pentagon Papers in 1971.
best_facts.why_surprising: A decision theorist became the century's most famous whistleblower.

best_facts.fact: Owning a coffee mug for a few minutes made students value it at 7.12 dollars, while would-be buyers offered 2.87.
best_facts.why_surprising: Ownership alone more than doubled the price.

best_facts.fact: A study about honesty, showing that signing at the top of a form reduces cheating, was itself based on fabricated data and retracted in 2021.
best_facts.why_surprising: The research on dishonesty was dishonest.

best_facts.fact: When two US nudge units' complete trial records were analysed, the average nudge worked at about a sixth of the strength reported in journals: 1.4 versus 8.7 percentage points.
best_facts.why_surprising: Publication bias had inflated the field's flagship tool.

best_facts.fact: In rural Udaipur, a 1 kg bag of lentils per shot raised full child immunisation from 6 percent (no programme) to 39 percent, and halved the cost per child.
best_facts.why_surprising: A bag of dal beat free vaccines on their own.

best_facts.fact: Shiller's book Irrational Exuberance came out in March 2000, the very month the dot-com bubble peaked.
best_facts.why_surprising: Its timing could hardly have been better.

best_facts.fact: The famous claim that the Schiphol urinal fly cut spillage by 80 percent was never measured; the manager called it 'very empirical'.
best_facts.why_surprising: The founding fable of nudging rests on a guess.

best_facts.fact: The 'hot hand fallacy', a textbook example of human bias for 30 years, was itself reversed in 2018 when economists found the original test was statistically biased.
best_facts.why_surprising: Experts on bias made a bias error.

best_facts.fact: Opt-out Austria had 99.98 percent effective organ-donor consent against about 12 percent in opt-in Germany.
The same Tamil Nadu sugarcane farmers scored worse on cognitive tests before harvest, when short of money, than after it.
best_facts.why_surprising: Poverty itself seems to tax the mind.

best_facts.fact: Amazon agreed in September 2025 to pay 2.5 billion dollars over the design of its Prime sign-up and cancellation screens.
best_facts.why_surprising: An interface, not a price, was the harm.

best_facts.fact: Harvard revoked Francesca Gino's tenure in May 2025, reportedly the first time it had done so since the 1940s.
best_facts.why_surprising: Tenure is almost never taken away.

best_facts.fact: Monthly gym members paid over 17 dollars per visit when a 10-visit pass would have cost 10 dollars a visit.
best_facts.why_surprising: People pay for the self they plan to become.

side_dish.title: Ulysses and the Sirens: the first commitment device
side_dish.body_md:
In Homer's Odyssey, the hero must sail past the Sirens, whose song lures sailors to wreck on their rocks. Ulysses wants to hear the song and survive. So he does something clever: he has his crew plug their ears with beeswax, then tie him to the mast, with orders to ignore anything he says and tie him tighter if he begs to be released. When the song comes, he does beg. They ignore him. Everyone lives.

Economists love this story because it is the cleanest picture of a **commitment device**: a choice made today, by your calm self, that removes options from your tempted future self. Thaler's cashew bowl is a small version. Save More Tomorrow is a pension version. So is a savings account you cannot touch until a date, a phone app that locks social media at night, or a bet with a friend that you will finish a project.

The interesting twist is that commitment only makes sense if you know you are weak. A perfectly rational person never needs to be tied to a mast. A naive person thinks they will resist and does not bother. The sophisticated person, who knows their future self will waver, pays to tie the knot. Behavioural economists call this being 'sophisticated' about present bias, and much of the work on saving, dieting and procrastination asks how to help people get there.

Try it today: choose one temptation and tie one knot.

offline_task.title: Run the anchoring experiment on three people
offline_task.body_md:
**Takes 10 minutes. You need a pen, paper and three people (family, friends, colleagues).**

1. Write two numbers on separate slips: **12** and **78**.
2. For each person, without letting them see the other slip, show one number (alternate between them). Say: 'Is the number of countries in Africa higher or lower than this number?'
3. Then ask: 'What is your best guess for how many countries there are in Africa?' Write down the guess next to the number they saw.
4. Compare. Did the people who saw 78 guess higher than those who saw 12? (Africa has 54 countries in the United Nations, but the right answer does not matter: the gap between the two groups does.)
5. Tell them afterwards, and ask whether they felt the number influenced them. Most will say no.

**Then notice anchors in your own day**: a 'was' price on a sale tag, the first salary figure in a negotiation, the 'suggested donation' on a form. For each one, ask: if I had not seen this number, what would I have guessed?
